label: copy-phase input token a (fed-back a, from recall step 2 on)
explanation: Token detector for the letter a as a fed-back input during the copy phase, i.e. the step right after the model has output an original a. On dev it fires on every such step with recall_idx >= 2 (precision 1.0, recall 0.97, mass recall 0.999). It does not fire on a during the original phase or on any other token. When a is the first original token (fed back at recall_idx 1, right after the delimiter step output) it fires only very weakly (~0.02-0.07 of max), and these steps are nearly all of the misses. In the examples, magnitude is lower when the a is fed back early in the copy (~0.4-0.5 of max at recall_idx 2) and near max at later positions; a second consecutive a is slightly weaker (~0.85) than the first.

issues: Minor wording problem, not systematic: the explanation says the feature fires 'only very weakly' when a is fed back at recall_idx 1. In fact, (phase==2)&(in_tok==a)&(recall_idx==1) has test precision 0.14, so it is silent on about 86% of those steps and very weak (0.01-0.08 of max) on the rest. These steps make up nearly all of the misses (2362 test steps, 0.1% of activation mass).

The claim that it 'does not fire on any other token' is true apart from scattered noise: about 14 dev activations on other tokens, plus 14 activations at orig_idx 8 in the original phase. All of it carries negligible mass.

Test misses show no false positives (0) and no systematic missed class except the a-at-recall_idx-1 case, which the explanation already covers. Test scores are P=1.0, R=0.969, F1=0.984, mass recall 0.999.

The magnitude claims match the examples: recall_idx 2 gives about 0.42-0.51, later positions give 0.8-1.0, and a second a in a row is about 0.82-0.89. These are qualitative and come from the examples only.
Dropping the recall_idx>=2 condition makes it worse (test F1 0.915, precision 0.84), so the original predicate is already the better one.
